purpose: Insulin human is used to control blood sugar levels in people with diabetes. It helps your body use sugar from the food you eat for energy. Keeping blood sugar in a healthy range helps prevent serious problems with your heart, kidneys, eyes, and nerves.
how_it_works: Your body normally makes a hormone called insulin that acts like a key, unlocking your cells so sugar from your blood can get inside and be used for energy. In diabetes, your body either does not make enough insulin or cannot use it well. Insulin human is a man-made version of this natural hormone that works just like the insulin your body would normally produce.
common_side_effects: The most common side effect is low blood sugar (hypoglycemia), which can make you feel shaky, sweaty, dizzy, confused, or very hungry. You may also notice redness, swelling, or a small lump at the injection site. Weight gain can also occur over time.
warnings: Low blood sugar (hypoglycemia) can be dangerous — always have a fast-acting sugar source like glucose tablets or juice nearby. Never skip meals after taking insulin. Tell your doctor about all other medicines you take, as many can affect how insulin works. Store insulin properly — unused insulin should be refrigerated, and never use insulin that looks cloudy or has particles if it is supposed to be clear. Alcohol can lower your blood sugar more than usual, so be careful.
typical_dosing: Dosing is very personal and set by your doctor based on your blood sugar levels, diet, and activity. It is given as an injection under the skin (subcutaneously) or, in some cases, through an IV in a hospital. Regular insulin (R) is usually taken 30 minutes before meals, while NPH insulin (N) is a longer-acting type taken once or twice a day. Always follow your doctor's exact instructions and never adjust your dose on your own.
